Backstreet abortions

By: Tarryn Crossman | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
With only 40% of state facilities that are supposed to offer legal abortions in South Africa actually offering the service there is a massive market for illegal/backstreet abortions.We are asking if termination is legal and free at state facilities until 20 weeks,
why are woman turning to these dangerous and costly methods? And why are these illegal operations so easily accessible, all it takes is a google search.


Further information:
We went undercover to three clinics that are advertised online and managed to get a medical abortion at 28 weeks. All the suppliers were very candid about the services they offer. The medical abortion they do uses the same medication offered at the state clinics it is just completely unmonitored and no scan or check up is done before you are given the drugs that will cause a miscarriage. No check is done afterwards either to make sure everything is out. The drugs are called CYTOTEX (MISOPROSTOL) Pfixer product. These are schedule 6 drugs.

Post taking the prescribed medication, the instructions we were given was to sit on a bucket and then let the baby fall into the plastic bag and throw it away. One clinic offered a Surgical procedure up until 4 months, which basically was explained as a cutting of the vagina to make space for the doctors hand to remove the baby. All the foetus’s/babies would be dead on delivery due the medication administered

The cost of an illegal termination is however the same as the cost to get an abortion at a private facility like Marie stopes. The misconception is that Marie stopes and other private facilities are more expensive.

The piece tells the story of how limited access to what should be a standard medical procedure has opened the door to a massive black market. And it asks why are woman not getting the service promised to them by the constitution?


Case study 1:
Had an illegal abortion in 2010. Detailed story about how the procure worked and has now created a network of woman who have been through the same thing
Educated, journalist. She tried Bara and they were so awful to her to she ran away and went to a downtown clinic that she thought was legal, but turned out to be extremely makeshift.

Case study 2
Went to various clinic they kept postponing her appointment finally in a panic she contacted one of the illegal guys and did the pills at home

Press Release:


Backstreet Abortions
Terminating a pregnancy has been legal in South Africa since 1996, but as some women get turned away from state health care facilities, they turn to the backstreets of Johannesburg - in illegal clinics for an abortion. In this special report, Carte Blanche goes undercover and reveals why some women are still choosing dodgy hotel rooms turned into makeshift hospital wards to terminate.
Producer: Tarryn Crossman
Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender


Script:







































Time code visual CHARACTER
00:00 Voice over In 2019 no woman should have to have an abortion in dodgy downtown back alleys.

But that is exactly what’s happening.

Gao: They didn’t say anything they just said lay down and it was extremely painful.

Anonymous: It’s scary and traumatic
00:17 Devi Link A woman in South African can legally choose to terminate her pregnancy up till 12 weeks. She doesn’t need to give a reason and doesn’t need anybody’s consent except her own unless she is under 12 years old. So why when termination is legal and supposed to be free at state facilities are so many women turning to back street abortions?
00:41 Voice over
For ZOE

When Zoey discovered she was pregnant, she tried to access a legal abortion, but she battled, even just to get an appointment at a local Gauteng clinic. She’s asked that we conceal her identity as her family still don’t know she had an abortion
00:53 Zoe interview When I got there the lady was not there, the door was closed I waited from around 12:00pm until 15:00pm. I went back on Thursday the following day... the next Thursday and we were told the lady is not available, and I was almost 12 weeks Pregnant. I kept going there, every time there was an excuse. I got to over 12 weeks I had lost hope in the government system
01:24 Voice over Gao tried at Charlotte Maxeke Johannesburg Academic Hospital to get a legal termination.
01:29 Gao Interview I told them look I think I’m about 5 weeks or 6 weeks pregnant and I would like to have. An abortion and the lady said sit down I will come back, and I think I wait for. About 3 hours and then she said the next available date I can’t remember how many months it was but when I calculated I would’ve by then been 6 or 7 months pregnant and I was like but. I can’t have an abortion then. She said well. There’s nothing I can do about it that’s the waiting list. I had already felt embarrassed by then so I also kind of felt resisted by then to push further. And so I left
02:01 Voice over Dr. Tlaleng Mofokeng runs DISA Health Clinic in Sandton which offers Sexual and Reproductive Health services for women.
Mofokeng says South African laws allow for two termination procedures – medical or ssurgical. Both have to be performed before 12 weeks. Between 13 – 20 weeks a woman has to provide specific reasons…but after 20 weeks, it will only be legal if the woman or the fetus’ lives are endangered.
02:31 Dr. Mofokeng Inter with Devi Dr. Mofokeng: A medical abortion is when you are using medication only, tablets. The other option is a surgical abortion. It also. Starts with a tablet, in the very similar sequence except that the surgical abortion involves emptying out the uterus using manual vacuum aspiration.

Devi: A survey that was conducted showed that only 4 out of every 10 public clinics should be offering termination services actually do.

Dr. Mofokeng: None of this is breaking news for us and it shouldn’t be breaking news for the department either. Women still do not know where to go to access termination and often. When they do go to a clinic. Or hospital or district facility often they are turned away. The security guard, the cleaners are turning patients away. So you have a system where everyone. Feels they have a right to tell women what to do with their bodies.

Dev: is it not surprising then that so many women do resort to. Legal backstreet abortion.

Dr. Mofokeng: It’s not surprising its such violence. There is no other way of doing it
03:32 Devi Link After doing an online search. We found 3 clinics in Johannesburg willing to perform. A termination as late as 28 weeks. So we took our Hidden cameras to see exactly how these back-street abortions operate.
03:47 Hidden camera

Voice over


We first visited a hidden office in downtown Johannesburg going by the name of Riverside Clinic where a “Dr. John” received us.
03:55 Dr. John Hidden Camera Dr. John: We use abortion pills to cause a miscarriage, we are looking at about 10 -12 pills. We don’t do it on the premises because its illegal. Two streets away from Lister there’s. A guest house it’s like a hotel so we have. A room where we stay with the patient until its done. Come in today, we can set up a time and then assist you
04:17 Voice over Nearby in the street, we met a man called Frank – he insisted we take abortion pills and call an Ambulance and pretend to be having a miscarriage.
04:24 Frank Hidden Camera Frank: I want the whole thing to be… by the time you’re on your way there, they can’t reverse the process. So its 5 then after 4 hours’ time another 5. If she hasn’t counted the weeks and its already 30 or 29, she’s still covered. What I just want is for us to hide this – the packaging

Lady: The packaging?

Frank: Because if someone sees this

Lady: They going to know?

Frank: They’re gonna know what we did

04:59 Voice over Our undercover operative met with Sam from Dr. Lerato’s abortion clinic who sold him 12 abortion pills for R1500
05:09 Sam hidden camera Lady: Why don’t they go to normal clinics? Why do they come to you?

Sam: they go to the queue after they sign, they give them an appointment to come back. Sometimes when you come back, they say come back another day until its growing up and they’re like – no now its growing up we can’t do this but if they come to us, we do it the day you want, like today. We even get nurses from the hospital, we get police, they know the laws and the come to us.
05:40 Voice over It wasn’t only pills on offer – “Dr. John” explained how he could perform a surgical abortion up to 4 months into the pregnancy.
05:48 Dr. John hidden camera Dr. John: We cut through the vagina, widen it then we have to use a speculum where my hand fits in order to detach the fetus off the body and then vacuum it out
06:03 Devi interview with Dr. Mofokeng Devi: This is a whole new level

Dr. Mofokeng: Even in a health facility even in a hospital it doesn’t happen in that way. So that’s very horrific, it’s very scary that someone could hear that and still trust that it’s okay. It tells you the amount of vulnerability and desperation that people are under because there is no way you can listen to that and think that’s okay. What pains me the most is that a trained health care professional with the right equipment and the right medication offering this service has one of the lowest complication rates safer than a colonoscopy.

Devi: This is what we were given,

Dr. Mofokeng: To me this is not uncommon. There are far too many. Pills and these are not the only pills we use. We only use 4 this is not safe there will. Be problems you can get urinal rapture again the unsuccessful rate means that the. Department spends more money dealing. With complication with unsafe procedures
07:02 Voice over Desperate to terminate her pregnancy Zoe got a number off a poster off the streets and met with a man who sold her 4 pills for R700.
07:11 Zoe I was desperate so I did what he told me. And he told me you need to… when you start bleeding you need sit on a bucket. There was a lot of blood coming out. I was with a. friend and she helped me because the fetus came out with an umbilical cord and everything so she helped me to cut the cord and I was still bleeding I knew that my life was in danger. I went to the hospital I got insulted by the nurses there but they did help me. They cleaned me
07:58 Devi and Dr. Mofokeng Devi: Is it only people who don’t have a lot of money who go to back street abortion?

Dr. Mofokeng: No and these people are very clever so they know when you park your BMW there at Ghandi Square that no this is the one that we charge R5000 so that also happens, they profile you. This is criminal activity.
08:17 Voice over A backstreet operator costs almost the same as a legitimate clinic but information to access these clinics is harder to find than illegal operators number on a wall. This is perpetuated by the fact that many clinics receive United States federal funding which comes with a gag rule which allows clinics to for abortions against cases of rape, incest’s or if a woman’s life is at risk and bars them to referring women to alternative clinics which is exactly how Gao found herself in a dodgy flat in Hilbrow
08:47 Gao interview Gao: I don’t know what you call those things that’s they put your legs on they had that to spread my legs, told to sit back and one of my ladies held me back, she did whatever she was doing it was extremely painful I didn’t know what she was doing. At some point I said stop I didn’t know what was. Happening and the lady holding me down continued. The remains of the pregnancy of the woman that went before me was still in the bucket or whatever they were using there and I did see them out whatever came out of me in there. I didn’t even see them clean whatever instrument they were using. Afterwards they said its done, just go home and take panado
09:23 Voice over Meisie Lerutla is a chief Director for Primary Health Care in Johannesburg
09:28 Devi and Meisie interview Devi: Is it a high incident of women coming into state hospitals who have tried to do backstreet abortions

Meisie: We do see woman that percent having tried to do an illegal abortion but I do no have the statistics that I can. Provide at this stage.

Devi: But enough to make you concerned?

Meisie: It is a concern,

Devi: Have you ever disciplined any staff members for making it difficult for a woman to have a termination? Has it ever happened?

Meisie: I have never had a case of that. Nature being reported to me.
09:58 Devi link The choice to terminate should never out a woman’s life to risk not in a country where abortion has been legal since 1996.
10:08 Voice over We returned to Johannesburg CBD to confront the three abortion clinics we had investigated undercover.
10:17 Devi on the street We here to see Dr. John, he has offices in this building across the road.
10:32 Devi at Dr. John offices Devi: Hello…
10:34 Voice over We waited for Dr. John for over an hour
10:37 Devi link After repeatedly calling Dr. John we then got a call from him saying that he knew what we were up he had seen the Television cameras
10:46 Voice over Next, we had planned to meet Sam, but after Dr. John was onto us Sam stopped taking our calls. Then Frank also suddenly stopped taking our calls.
Subsequently, we gave all three another chance to tell their story, but none of them took up the offer.
11:03 Devi and Meisie Devi: What is the department doing to stop those individuals form operating?

Meisie: The first part is us offering the service and that we are doing and the second part…

Devi: No you are not doing it, to the extend

Meisie: we are not optimally… yeah yes

Devi: yes, so you should not be saying that you are doing it especially when we know that the majority of woman are opting to have backstreet. Abortions so that cannot be part of your argument I’m afraid.

Meisie: the other thing that we are doing as department, whenever we are made aware of a facility that is offering the back street. Abortions we immediately report them to the law enforcement
11:45 Dr. Mofokeng It’s the only medical procedure in this country that has an ACT, there is no ACT that determines any other health care. Services yet on that one we fail on an executive level, we fail on administratively we fail clinically, we literally failing woman at every single level

- End

metadata.Summary: With only 40% of state facilities that are supposed to offer legal abortions in South Africa actually offering the service there is a massive market for illegal/backstreet abortions.We are asking if termination is legal and free at state facilities until 20 weeks, why are woman turning to these dangerous and costly methods? And why are these illegal operations so easily accessible, all it takes is a google search.
metadata.Further information: We went undercover to three clinics that are advertised online and managed to get a medical abortion at 28 weeks. All the suppliers were very candid about the services they offer. The medical abortion they do uses the same medication offered at the state clinics it is just completely unmonitored and no scan or check up is done before you are given the drugs that will cause a miscarriage. No check is done afterwards either to make sure everything is out. The drugs are called CYTOTEX (MISOPROSTOL) Pfixer product. These are schedule 6 drugs. Post taking the prescribed medication, the instructions we were given was to sit on a bucket and then let the baby fall into the plastic bag and throw it away. One clinic offered a Surgical procedure up until 4 months, which basically was explained as a cutting of the vagina to make space for the doctors hand to remove the baby. All the foetus’s/babies would be dead on delivery due the medication administered The cost of an illegal termination is however the same as the cost to get an abortion at a private facility like Marie stopes. The misconception is that Marie stopes and other private facilities are more expensive. The piece tells the story of how limited access to what should be a standard medical procedure has opened the door to a massive black market. And it asks why are woman not getting the service promised to them by the constitution? Case study 1: Had an illegal abortion in 2010. Detailed story about how the procure worked and has now created a network of woman who have been through the same thing Educated, journalist.
